title: Scientific Investigation

standard_text: Pupils plan and carry out fair tests, identify variables, make predictions, collect and record data in tables and graphs, calculate averages, and draw conclusions supported by evidence. (summary of the Basic Science and Technology curriculum, Primary 4, theme: Science and Development)
meta_desc: Free Primary 4 Basic Science and Technology worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Science and Development): fair tests, variables, predictions, tables and graphs, averages and conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one thing and keep the rest the same.
key_sub: A conclusion must match the evidence.
body_html:
How to think about it

A scientific investigation answers a question by testing. In a fair test, you change only one variable (the independent variable), measure another (the dependent variable), and keep all other variables the same (controlled variables).

Record results in a table and show them in a graph. Repeat trials and find the average. Look for patterns and write a conclusion that the data support; explain any results that do not fit.

Example

Testing which ball bounces highest: what must stay the same?

Fair test

Answer: the drop height and the floor

Example

Results 10, 12, 14 cm. Average?

Add and divide by 3

Answer: 12 cm

Common mistakes

  • Changing two things at once.
  • Writing a conclusion from one trial.
  • Ignoring results that do not fit without explaining them.

items.q: A table has the heading 'Time'. What is missing?
items.e: Always write units in table headings.

items.q: Which equipment measures time accurately?
items.e: Time in seconds.

items.q: Which of these questions can be answered by a fair test?
c: Does the height of a ramp change how far a toy car rolls?
What is the best footy team?
Is science more fun than art?
Which day of the week is the best?
items.e: A testable question changes one thing and measures another.

items.q: What is a fair test?
c: a test where only one variable is changed and the others are kept the same
items.e: Change one thing.

items.q: Which of these questions CANNOT be answered by a scientific test?
c: Does the amount of sunlight change how tall bean plants grow?
Do people like the smell of eucalyptus?
Does salt water freeze faster than tap water?
Does the type of surface change how far a ball rolls?
items.e: Opinions cannot be measured with a fair test.

items.e: A testable question changes one thing and measures another.

items.q: What is a prediction?
c: what you think will happen, based on what you already know
items.e: Make a prediction before the test.

items.q: A class investigates how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls. Which is the independent variable (the one you change)?
c: the same car and the same floor surface
items.e: Change: the height of the ramp. Measure: how far the car rolls. Keep the same: the same car and the same floor surface.

items.q: Investigation: “Does salt water make iron nails rust faster than tap water?” Which variable should be changed?
c: the same kind of nail, the same amount of water and the same place
how much rust forms in a week
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The nail in salt water had the most rust after a week.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The black bottle got hotter because dark colours absorb more light.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: A class investigates how the amount of light affects the growth of wheat seedlings. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
c: the same mass and the same starting angle
the same soil and the same amount of water
items.e: Change: the amount of light. Measure: the height of the seedlings. Keep the same: the same soil and the same amount of water.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the amount of sunlight affect how tall a sunflower grows?” Which variable should be changed?

items.q: Investigation: “Does the amount of sunlight affect how tall a sunflower grows?” What should be measured?

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the number of birds of each kind seen in a garden?
items.e: Bar chart: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the arm span and height of every pupil in a class?

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the height of a sunflower measured every week?

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the temperature of a cup of tea every 2 minutes as it cools?
